title: Coherent Pastoral Care
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart argues that pastoral care in schools rarely lacks commitment but often lacks coherence, and that coherence is a matter of deliberate design rather than goodwill. He breaks pastoral care into distinct subdomains (safeguarding, behaviour, attendance, wellbeing, counselling, family support, transitions, careers and student voice) and defines integration as designing how responsibility, information and authority move between them. When those decisions are left implicit, he argues, teams compensate through effort, relationships and escalation to the headteacher. Revising his earlier Run, Serve and Change framing into levels of work, he locates coherence chiefly in the middle layer of systems such as shared thresholds, referral and handover pathways, multi-domain case coordination and leadership forums that settle recurring tensions once. He closes with the settled decisions leaders must make, including when concerns move between domains and which judgements should never be made alone, so that day-to-day pastoral work can stay human and sustainable.
points: Hart treats pastoral care as a whole made of distinct subdomains whose relationships must be designed rather than merged.
Integration is made concrete as decisions about precedence, information-sharing, transfer of responsibility, fixed versus flexible thresholds, and how emotional load is held structurally.
When integration is left implicit, he argues, pastoral teams compensate through individual effort and escalation to the headteacher.
Coherence is built in the middle layer of shared thresholds, referral pathways, case coordination and leadership forums, not in policies or people alone.
Leaders' Change work is to settle a small set of integrative questions once so Serve systems run cleanly and Run work remains sustainable.
quotes: Pastoral care in schools is rarely lacking in commitment. We all know colleagues who are deeply invested in student wellbeing, safeguarding, student voice or careers guidance and they do a fantastic job of contributing to a holistic education.

A coherent system allows them to remain distinct while working in relation to one another. Integration is the work of designing how those relations operate. The task is not to merge these domains, but to design how responsibility, information and authority move between them.

These are design decisions and when they are made clearly, pastoral care feels purposeful. But when they are left implicit, the team compensates through effort, relationships and escalation to the Headteacher.

Leaders don’t experience pastoral care as abstract modes; they experience it as work happening at different levels. Some work is about settling decisions once so they stop being renegotiated. Some work is about putting systems in place so uncertainty, coordination and judgement are held by the organisation rather than individuals.

In practice, there will be multiple people doing this work, from the Headteacher to teachers to specialist roles such as counsellors. But someone needs to hold responsibility for the domain as a whole, so the necessary integration work is visible and owned.
It is not policies or people that make the work coherent. Coherence requires structures. This is where integration actually happens in practice.
Coherence in pastoral care cannot rely on goodwill or vocation. It is the result of careful design and ongoing integration work.
